name: Fexofenadine
summary: Fexofenadine is a non-drowsy antihistamine that relieves allergy symptoms such as those of hay fever and hives by blocking the effects of histamine. Some people still feel sleepy or dizzy, and the NHS advises against driving, cycling or using tools or machinery if that happens. Swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing or fainting can be signs of a serious allergic reaction and need urgent medical help, through 999 or A&E.
usedFor: Allergy symptoms such as a runny nose, sneezing, and red, itchy or watery eyes, including hay fever
Hives, with their itching and redness
Long-term hives with no identified cause (chronic idiopathic urticaria), as stated in the leaflet for the branded product Telfast
Conjunctivitis, eczema, insect bite and sting reactions and some food allergies, which the NHS lists among its uses
howItWorks: Fexofenadine blocks the effects of histamine, a substance in the body that drives allergy symptoms. A 2024 review describes it as a non-sedating, second-generation H1 antihistamine. The NHS says it seems less likely to cause sleepiness than other non-drowsy antihistamines.
onset: The NHS says relief usually starts within 1 to 2 hours.

common: Headache, feeling sleepy, feeling sick and feeling dizzy are the common side effects the NHS lists.
Although fexofenadine is classed as non-drowsy, some people feel quite sleepy, and the NHS advises not driving, cycling or using tools or machinery while sleepy or dizzy.
serious: Swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing or fainting can signal a serious allergic reaction and need urgent medical help through 999 or A&E.

cautions: Grapefruit, orange and apple juice can reduce how well fexofenadine works, and MedlinePlus advises taking it with water rather than fruit juice.
Antacids containing aluminium or magnesium reduce how much fexofenadine is absorbed, and leaflets advise leaving a gap between the two.
A leaflet states that apalutamide, a prostate cancer medicine, may decrease the effect of fexofenadine.

Leaflets advise asking a doctor or pharmacist first about people with liver or kidney problems, heart disease, or older age, and one leaflet notes that antihistamines such as fexofenadine may make the heart beat faster.

One leaflet advises against taking fexofenadine in pregnancy unless necessary and says it is not recommended while breastfeeding, while other leaflets tell pregnant or breastfeeding women to ask a doctor or pharmacist first.
A known allergy to fexofenadine or any of the other ingredients is a reason not to take it.
The NHS says fexofenadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.
monitoring: No routine tests or monitoring are described in the patient sources reviewed, and the NHS says it is best taken only for as long as it is needed.

sections.heading: What is fexofenadine used for?
sections.body:
Fexofenadine is an antihistamine medicine that relieves the symptoms of allergies. The NHS lists hay fever, conjunctivitis, eczema, hives, insect bite and sting reactions and some food allergies among the problems it is used for. MedlinePlus describes it as treating allergy symptoms such as a runny nose, sneezing, and red, itchy or watery eyes, as well as itching and redness caused by hives.

A leaflet for the branded product Telfast says it is used in adults and adolescents aged 12 and over to relieve itching, swelling and rashes from long-term allergic skin reactions known as chronic idiopathic urticaria. MedlinePlus has a separate page for products that combine fexofenadine with pseudoephedrine, which are different products from fexofenadine on its own.

sections.heading: How does fexofenadine work?
sections.body:
Fexofenadine blocks histamine, a substance in the body that drives allergy symptoms. The NHS says that by blocking the effects of histamine it reduces the symptoms, and that people should start to feel better within 1 to 2 hours. A 2024 review describes it as a non-sedating, second-generation H1 antihistamine.

The NHS classes fexofenadine as non-drowsy and says it seems less likely to cause sleepiness than other non-drowsy antihistamines. It also says fexofenadine is unlikely to cause harm when used for a long time, though it is best taken only for as long as it is needed.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of fexofenadine?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headaches, feeling sleepy, feeling sick and feeling dizzy as the common side effects. Fexofenadine is classed as a non-drowsy antihistamine, but some people still feel quite sleepy. The NHS advises not driving, cycling or using tools or machinery while feeling sleepy or dizzy. Leaflets say fexofenadine is unlikely to affect the ability to drive or use machinery, but advise checking first that the tablets do not cause sleepiness or dizziness.

Swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing or fainting can be signs of a serious allergic reaction and need urgent medical help. In an emergency the route is 999 or A&E.

sections.heading: Fexofenadine with food, drink and other medicines
sections.body:
The NHS says grapefruit, orange and apple juice can reduce how well fexofenadine works. MedlinePlus likewise advises taking it with water rather than with fruit juices such as orange, grapefruit or apple juice. The NHS also recommends avoiding alcohol.

Antacids containing aluminium or magnesium reduce how much fexofenadine is absorbed, so leaflets advise leaving a gap between the two. A leaflet states that apalutamide, a prostate cancer medicine, may decrease the effect of fexofenadine. The NHS says fexofenadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

sections.heading: Who can take fexofenadine, and who needs extra care?
sections.body:
Tablets for adults and children aged 12 and over are sold over the counter from pharmacies and supermarkets, while tablets for children under 12 are only available on prescription from a doctor. Leaflets advise talking to a doctor or pharmacist first about liver or kidney problems, heart disease or older age. One leaflet notes that fexofenadine, like other antihistamines, may make the heart beat faster.

One leaflet advises against taking fexofenadine in pregnancy unless necessary and says it is not recommended while breastfeeding, while other leaflets tell pregnant or breastfeeding women to ask a doctor or pharmacist first. An NHS Scotland pharmacy protocol lists pregnancy and breastfeeding among the reasons not to supply it through that service. A known allergy to fexofenadine or any of its other ingredients is a reason not to take it. Leaflets differ in wording between products, so the leaflet that comes with a particular product applies to it.

faqs.a: The NHS classes fexofenadine as non-drowsy and says it seems less likely to cause sleepiness than other non-drowsy antihistamines. Even so, some people feel quite sleepy or dizzy, and the NHS advises not driving, cycling or using tools or machinery if that happens.

faqs.q: Can fruit juice be drunk with fexofenadine?
faqs.a: The NHS says grapefruit, orange and apple juice can reduce how well fexofenadine works. MedlinePlus advises taking it with water rather than fruit juice. The NHS also recommends avoiding alcohol.
The NHS says people should start to feel better within 1 to 2 hours. It says fexofenadine is unlikely to cause harm when used for a long time, but it is best taken only for as long as it is needed.

faqs.q: Can fexofenadine be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: Tablets for adults and children aged 12 and over are sold over the counter from pharmacies and supermarkets. Tablets for children under 12 are only available with a prescription from a doctor.
The NHS says fexofenadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

faqs.q: Can fexofenadine be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Leaflet wording differs between products: one advises against taking it in pregnancy unless necessary and says it is not recommended while breastfeeding, while others tell pregnant or breastfeeding women to ask a doctor or pharmacist first. A GP or pharmacist can advise on an individual situation.
